notes:
I ran out of searches before covering the whole chapter. Verses 19–22 come almost entirely from one source (Guzik), and I found nothing on vv. 30–31. I found no Orthodox source and no prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter. One whole-chapter commentary (Clarke on studylight.org) wouldn't load, so I only have the parts quoted in search results.

## Traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1**
- Precept Austin reads "at that time" as tying the illness to Jeroboam going on ordaining false priests in ch. 13. It quotes Lumby: the writer "connects the sickness of Jeroboam's son with the events which have been narrated in the previous chapter in the nature of a divine judgement." https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-14-commentary
- The name Abijah means "my father is Yah(weh)." Precept Austin thinks this may show a showy claim by Jeroboam. It also points out that Rehoboam's son has the same name (Abijam, v. 31), which can be confusing. Same URL.
- Guzik notes that even kings face ordinary trouble. He quotes Wiseman: people commonly asked prophets about health. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-14/

**v. 2**
- Guzik: in a crisis Jeroboam turned to the true God, because he knew idols couldn't help. But he also knew he had rejected God's prophets, so he sent his wife in disguise. He quotes F.B. Meyer on the folly of thinking a prophet could see the future but not through a disguise. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-14/
- Precept Austin finds it striking that Ahijah, a true prophet, stayed in the north. It suggests God had him stationed there to provide a lifeline to Jeroboam if he were willing to humble himself. It quotes Dale Ralph Davis: Jeroboam had ignored the "David-standard" Ahijah gave him (11:37–38) and probably expected the prophet to disapprove. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-14-commentary
- Matthew Henry: Jeroboam never asked Ahijah about setting up the calves. He only came to him in trouble, when the gods he served could give him no relief. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ki/1Ki_014.cfm
- Constable: he probably chose Ahijah because Ahijah had given him a favourable word before (11:29–39). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/14-13.html

**v. 3**
- Guzik: Jeroboam didn't ask for prayer. He treated the prophet as a fortuneteller instead of seeking him as a man of God. He quotes Matthew Henry's line that most people would rather hear their fortune than their faults. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-14/
- Barnes: the gifts were chosen to deceive, the kind of thing a poor country person would bring. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/14-4.htm Coffman calls it a paltry gift from a king, fitting her pose as a farmer's wife. https://studylight.org/commentaries/bcc/1-kings-14.html
- Constable: Jeroboam may have hoped the gift would win the prophet over, as he had won over the old prophet of Bethel. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/14-13.html

**v. 4**
- Cambridge Bible: the same phrase about the eyes is used of Eli (1 Sam 4:15). It describes an eye that no longer reacts to light. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/14-4.htm
- Barnes: Jeroboam was counting on Ahijah's blindness (compare Isaac in Gen 27). Benson/Henry: Ahijah was blind, yet still received visions, which don't need bodily eyes. Same URL.
- BibleHub's study notes: by going to Shiloh, where the tabernacle once stood, she bypasses Bethel and Dan. That quietly admits those shrines have no real authority. https://biblehub.com/1_kings/14-4.htm
- Precept Austin: the prophet's eyes failed, but his spiritual sight was perfect. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-14-commentary

**v. 5**
- Guzik: neither the disguise nor the blindness mattered, because God told Ahijah the truth. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-14/
- Precept Austin: she came to ask the prophet *about* her son, not to ask anything *for* him. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-14-commentary

**v. 6**
- Guzik: she learned two things. The news was bad, and Ahijah was the one sent, by God, not she by her husband. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-14/
- Benson and Poole: calling her by name exposed their folly in trying to hide from God, and it assured her the message was true. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/14-6.htm
- Geneva note: God often discloses to his own the craft and subtilty of the wicked. Same URL.
- Kelly: "What a humiliation!" https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/14-13.html

**vv. 7–8**
- Guzik quotes Poole: David also sinned, but he kept to true worship and repented, while Jeroboam was stubborn and wouldn't change. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-14/

**v. 9**
- Guzik: Jeroboam became the measuring line for Israel's bad kings to come. He reads "cast Me behind your back" as deep contempt, citing Ezek 23:35. He quotes Dilday on the contrast: God putting our sins behind His back is good news, but a person putting God behind their back is tragic. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-14/
- Coffman says "other gods" disproves those who treat the calves as symbols of Yahweh (see Other views). https://studylight.org/commentaries/bcc/1-kings-14.html

**vv. 10–11**
- Guzik: Jeroboam could have had a lasting dynasty but threw away God's promise. "Every male" is literally "he who urinates against the wall" (quoting Patterson and Austel). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-14/
- Kitto: the voice that once announced Jeroboam's rise now announced his house's fall. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-14-commentary

**v. 12**
- Kitto describes a mother torn between hurrying home and holding back, since her arrival would mean the boy's death. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-14-commentary

**v. 13**
- Keil & Delitzsch: of all the males in the house, only he would be properly buried, because something good toward Yahweh was found in him. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/14-3.html
- Guzik: his death was a mercy, since compared with what was coming he was blessed to die honoured. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-14/
- Kitto says the same: God can afflict no less by what he spares than by what he takes. Death took the boy away from the evil to come. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-14-commentary
- What was the "good thing"? Gill reports a Jewish tradition that he removed the guards who stopped Israelites going to the feasts in Jerusalem. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/14-13.html Precept Austin calls such traditions speculation. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-14-commentary

**v. 14**
- Guzik groups vv. 12–16 as a near judgment and a distant one. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-14/

**vv. 15–16**
- Guzik: the exile was fulfilled about 300 years later. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-14/
- Keil & Delitzsch: Ahijah announced exile so that the people who joined the idolatry, not just Jeroboam, would see how severe the judgment was. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/14-3.html
- Cogan (in Precept Austin): the prophecy moves from Jeroboam's personal sin to the whole nation's. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-14-commentary

**vv. 17–18**
- Guzik: the far-off prophecy of exile was proved true by the exact fulfilment of the near one. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-14/
- Precept Austin: Jeroboam should have repented after seeing this, but by now he was enslaved to his wickedness. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-14-commentary
- Matthew Henry: Tirzah means "delightful," yet death couldn't be kept out. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ki/1Ki_014.cfm

**vv. 19–20**
- Guzik cites 2 Chr 13:20 (the LORD struck Jeroboam down). He quotes Trapp: Jeroboam didn't die an ordinary death. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-14/

**vv. 21–22**
- Guzik: these were sins of idolatry, like an unfaithful spouse committing spiritual adultery, and that is why they stirred God's jealousy. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-14/

**v. 24**
- Guzik: these were prostitutes connected with idol worship. Deut 23:17–18 uses the term in contrast to the female form. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-14/
- Keil & Delitzsch take the word as a collective covering both males and females. A Pulpit-type note thinks they were probably of Canaanite or Phoenician origin. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/14-24.htm

**vv. 25–26**
- Guzik: 2 Chronicles 12 and archaeology both confirm the raid. Chronicles adds that Rehoboam had forsaken the law, that Shemaiah led the leaders to repent, and that Jerusalem was spared but made subject to Shishak. He quotes Wiseman: the campaign is recorded on the temple reliefs at Karnak. Guzik also notes that Solomon's gold shields were for display, not battle, an example of image over substance. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-14/
- BibleHub's Q&A: the loss was covenant discipline, not random politics. https://biblehub.com/q/Why_replace_shields_with_bronze_in_1_Kings.htm

**vv. 27–28**
- Guzik quotes Knapp: the bronze shields were a sad attempt to keep up appearances. Knapp applies this to churches that have lost their power and cover it with ritual or showy revivalism. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-14/
- BibleHub's study notes: bronze in place of gold reflects spiritual decline. https://biblehub.com/study/1_kings/14-27.htm

**v. 29**
- The Catholic Encyclopedia notes that the author of Kings drew Rehoboam's story from the "book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah." https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/Third-and-Fourth-Books-of-Kings

## Where Protestant traditions differ
I didn't find any real disagreement between traditions on this chapter. What I found was different emphases on v. 13:
- **Baptist (Spurgeon):** the "good thing" was real grace worked by the Spirit, with faith implied, since without it nothing in him would have been good towards God. Even a small "good thing" holds every good thing in seed. https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/abijah-or-some-good-thing-towards-the-lord He also calls the queen an Egyptian princess and an idolater. https://biblehub.com/sermons/auth/spurgeon/abijah_or_some_good_thing_towards_the_lord.htm
- **Garner-Howes (Baptist):** Abijah was the only member of the king's family fit to die. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/1-kings-14.html
- **Methodist (Adam Clarke):** God respects even a little good, because it is a seed from himself. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/1-kings-14.html

## Other views
- **v. 9, modern scholarship:** Coffman argues against present-day commentators who see the golden bulls as symbols of Yahweh or pedestals for Him. He says Ahijah calls them "other gods." https://studylight.org/commentaries/bcc/1-kings-14.html (This comes from Coffman's side; I didn't read the scholars themselves.)
- **v. 24, modern scholarship:** Bible Odyssey questions the usual "temple prostitute" translation. It says the masculine *qadesh* can easily be understood as a priest given its frequent association with temple practices. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/temple-prostitute-word-study/
- **v. 25, Catholic:** the Catholic Encyclopedia says Shishak (Sesac) invaded at the invitation of Jeroboam. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/08344a.htm It also says Megiddo was taken in the same campaign, according to the Karnak lists. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/09526a.htm
